questions.question: What does the integral test link?
options: Convergence of a series and of a related improper integral.
The derivative of a function and its maximum
The value of an integral and the exact sum of every series.
The domain of a function and its codomain

questions.question: Which condition is required for the function in the integral test?
options: It is constant and undefined at $1$.
It takes only the values $0$ and $1$

questions.question: Why does $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^2}$ converge?
options: Because the integral test gives its exact sum

questions.question: Why does $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}$ diverge?
options: Because the terms are all zero
Because the integral test gives a finite exact sum

questions.question: What does the proposition define as $a_n$?
What does the integral test provide?
options: The exact value of every infinite series.
A convergence comparison, not the sum's value.
A rule that works without monotonicity
A method only for finite sums

questions.question: Suppose the required conditions of the integral test hold and $\displaystyle\int_1^{\infty}f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ converges. What follows?
options: The test gives the exact value of $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty}f(n)$

questions.question: Suppose the required conditions of the integral test hold and $\displaystyle\int_1^{\infty}f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ diverges. What follows?
options: The test gives the exact sum

questions.question: Which missing assumption would make use of the integral test unsafe?
options: The series is written with the symbol $\sum$
Nonnegativity or monotone decrease may fail.
The variable in the integral is called $x$.

questions.question: Under the integral test hypotheses on $f$, what is the conclusion about the sequence $\left(\sum_{i=1}^n f(i)-\int_1^n f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\right)_{n=1}^\infty$?
options: It is always equal to zero

questions.question: A student applies the integral test and then reports the exact value of $\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty}f(n)$ from the integral comparison alone. What is the issue?
options: The integral test never concerns infinite series.
The integral must always equal the sum
Convergence information, not the exact value of the sum.
The function must take only integer values

questions.question: Which conclusion is justified for the harmonic series using the integral test example?
options: It diverges because the corresponding improper integral $\displaystyle\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x$ diverges
It converges because its terms tend to zero
It converges because the integral test gives a finite sum
It cannot be compared with an improper integral

questions.question: What kind of function is required for the integral test?
What does the integral test compare an infinite series with?
options: A maximum on a closed interval

questions.question: Does the integral test give the exact value of the series sum?
options: Yes, it always gives the sum exactly
Only when the function is increasing
No, it provides a comparison for convergence

questions.question: Which improper integral is paired with $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{n^3}$ by the integral test?
If $f(x)=1/x^2$, which property needed for the test holds on $[1,+\infty)$?
If $\displaystyle\int_1^\infty f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ converges under the test hypotheses, what happens to $\sum_{n=1}^\infty f(n)$?
Why is monotone decrease important in the integral test?
options: It makes every series have sum $0$
It allows comparison with rectangle areas.
It removes the need for nonnegativity.

questions.question: Under the test hypotheses, if $\displaystyle\int_1^\infty f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ diverges, what can be concluded?
options: The series has only finitely many terms
